extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent applicants, and patent practitioners (USPTO guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether claims to nature-based products, compositions, processes, or assemblies are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the Step 1/Step 2A/Step 2B framework and the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis. Includes illustrative fact patterns and examples of structural, functional, and chemical/physical differences that may render a claim eligible or ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category, e.g., a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (Step 1: YES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim falls into a statutory category, proceed to analyze whether it is directed to a judicial exception (laws/natural principles/phenomena/products of nature) under the Step 2A/2B framework. Examples label compositions and processes as statutory categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify nature-based product versus non-nature-based claim focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the claim is focused on a nature-based product (a product of nature or a nature-derived substance) or is instead focused on an assembly/process/practical application that is not the product per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is focused on a product per se (e.g., isolated/purified molecule, cell, or naturally occurring organism) analyze as nature-based; if the claim as a whole is directed to an assembly or practical application (e.g., firework assembly, method of treatment), it may not be necessary to apply the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (core Step 2A test for nature-based products)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a nature-based product, analyze whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' from any naturally occurring counterpart(s) in their natural state (structural, functional, or other properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed product has such marked differences, it is not a 'product of nature' exception (Step 2A: NO) and may be eligible; if not, it is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires Step 2B analysis. Examples explain comparing combinations to individual components when no natural counterpart to the combination exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare combination claims to natural counterparts appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claimed product is a combination of multiple natural components, compare the claimed combination to naturally occurring counterpart(s): if the combination as claimed does not occur in nature, compare to the individual components in their natural states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the combination exhibits properties (e.g., explosiveness, slower spoiling, synergistic fermentation) that are markedly different from the components individually, those properties support eligibility (examples: gunpowder, pomelo juice with preservative, yogurt starter culture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural differences as grounds for marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in chemical or physical structure (e.g., different chemical structure, crystalline form, different glycan) can demonstrate 'markedly different characteristics' from the natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: addition/removal of functional groups (5-methyl/deoxy derivative), tetrahedral vs hexagonal-pyramidal crystals, high-mannose vs bacillosamine N-glycan. Structural uniqueness that prevents tying up natural usage supports Step 2A: NO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional differences as grounds for marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in biological or functional properties (e.g., new biological activities, altered infectivity, improved bioavailability, different half-life) can demonstrate a marked difference from naturally occurring counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 5-methyl amazonic acid stimulating hair growth, genetically modified bacteria degrading additional hydrocarbons, cell populations enabling tissue regeneration, or mixtures changing host-range infectivity. Functional changes created by human intervention are strong evidence of marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical/physical property differences as grounds for marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Alterations in chemical or physical properties (e.g., solubility, stability, explosive behavior, spoilage rate) can show marked differences from what naturally occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: amazonic acid is insoluble in water in nature but forms a stable aqueous composition with a solubilizing agent; pomelo juice with preservative spoils more slowly. Such property changes support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that encompass both natural and non-natural embodiments are problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim covers embodiments that are identical to naturally occurring material as well as embodiments that are altered, the claim may fail the 'markedly different characteristics' test because it includes natural forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a broad claim to 'amazonic acid' that includes both natural and purified forms is ineligible because some embodiments are identical to nature; narrowing to only structurally/phenotypically distinct forms can render claim eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claim treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, a product-by-process claim is not limited to the process steps but is limited to the product's structure as implied by those steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the product produced by the recited process has structural characteristics that are markedly different from the natural product, the claim can be eligible (e.g., product-by-process yielding deoxyamazonic acid equivalent to the structurally distinct molecule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification or isolation alone is insufficient to show marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely isolating or purifying a naturally occurring product (without any resulting marked structural/functional/property changes) does not render it patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: purified amazonic acid that is structurally and functionally identical to the natural molecule is a 'product of nature' exception; isolation/purification that does not change characteristics leads to Step 2A: YES and likely rejection under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures where components are unchanged vs mixtures that change components
rubrics_metrics.description: If components in a claimed mixture remain unchanged (e.g., separate bacteria in a kit), the claim may be directed to a product of nature; if mixing produces changed characteristics (synergy, new properties), it may show marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a kit containing separate bacterial species is ineligible because they are not combined; a starter culture where mixing produces lower-fat yogurt or faster fermentation is eligible because the mixture has different functional properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims focused on practical application (methods of treatment/practical application) are analyzed as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Process claims that focus on a practical application of a nature-based product (e.g., treating a disease) rather than claiming the product itself are often not directed to the judicial exception and need not undergo the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: methods of treating cancer by administering amazonic acid were analyzed as not directed to the product per se and thus eligible (Step 2A: NO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional elements can provide 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), evaluate whether additional elements, alone or in combination, add 'significantly more' to transform the claim into eligible subject matter (Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements that improve technology or add meaningful limitations (e.g., cores enveloped by polymeric layer producing colon release and improved bioavailability; scaffold + cells improving tissue regeneration) can supply 'significantly more'. Generic, well-understood, routine elements (e.g., generic containers) typically do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic, well-understood, routine, conventional elements do not add 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that are well-understood, routine, and conventional in the relevant field—especially when recited at a high level of generality—do not transform an ineligible claim into eligible subject matter under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: recitation of a generic container to hold cells is routine and does not add significantly more; thus a claim to a cell population 'in a container' remained directed to an exception and ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural uniqueness that prevents preemption supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed molecule or product that is structurally unique and does not preempt others from using the natural product supports eligibility because it does not tie up the natural product's future uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 5-methyl amazonic acid is a unique molecule distinct from amazonic acid and therefore not a 'product of nature' exception; distinct molecules that do not prevent others from using the natural product are favorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenotypic differences created by human intervention count as marked differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenotypic changes in biological materials that result from applicant's manipulations (not occurring by nature) can demonstrate marked differences from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pacemaker cells expressing marker Z with increased oxygen utilization due to culture conditions, or genetically modified bacteria with extra plasmids leading to new degradative abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in genetic information/sequence or percent-identity claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications to nucleic acid sequences (substitution modifications) or claims limited to sequences with specified percent identity (e.g., ≥90% identity to SEQ ID NO: 1) can indicate structural/genetic differences sufficient for eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include modified Gene W sequences with substitutions; silent changes may or may not affect characteristics, but percent-identity limitations and sequence-based limitations can narrow claims away from natural sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silent (synonymous) modifications may nonetheless affect characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Even nucleotide substitutions that are silent at the protein level can affect nucleic acid characteristics (transcription rate, splicing) and thus may contribute to marked differences in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance notes that some silent modifications affect properties of nucleic acids and should be evaluated for their impact on characteristics relative to natural counterparts.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claimed combination does not exist in nature, possibility of rare natural occurrence does not bar eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere theoretical possibility that a similar composition might arise rarely in nature does not render a composition nonpatentable; the examiner should determine whether the particular mixture exists in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Myriad: possibility of rare natural occurrence does not defeat eligibility if claim is otherwise markedly different; unless examiner can show the particular mixture exists in nature, eligibility can stand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and claim language may limit scope to avoid encompassing natural forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit definitions in the specification (e.g., defining 'purified Antibiotic L' to mean only tetrahedral crystal form or specific glycan) can limit the claim scope to non-natural embodiments and support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of clear claim limitations/definitions that exclude naturally occurring forms (e.g., crystal form, glycan type, percent identity, phenotype markers) helps avoid covering natural counterparts and supports Step 2A: NO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures that produce new inter-component interactions can be markedly different
rubrics_metrics.description: When components interact in the claimed mixture to produce new behaviors (e.g., altered growth rates, new host-range infectivity, synergistic fermentation), those emergent properties can constitute marked differences from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: certain Rhizobium strains when mixed infect additional plant species; mixed pacemaker cell populations interact to change growth rates enabling tissue regeneration; these emergent interactions support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims limited to particular useful applications may amount to 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting a claim to a particular useful application of a nature-based product—where the combination does more than generally link exceptions together—can provide 'significantly more' and render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pacemaker cells plus scaffold facilitating faster tissue regeneration is tied to a specific application and was found to add significantly more (Step 2B: YES).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a natural principle or property is not patentable by itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering qualities or properties of naturally occurring organisms or components (e.g., non-inhibition between strains) is a discovery of nature's handiwork and, without meaningful additional inventive application, is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Funk Brothers: aggregation or packaging of naturally occurring species that performs as nature intended does not make the claim patent-eligible if no marked difference or significant additional inventive contribution is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claim must be considered under broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are analyzed under their broadest reasonable interpretation for eligibility purposes; if under that interpretation the claim encompasses natural forms it may be ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples repeatedly apply broadest reasonable interpretation when determining whether claims cover natural embodiments (e.g., Antibiotic L claim covering both natural and modified forms was ineligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of well-understood conventional materials or steps at high generality will not rescue a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting conventional component(s) (e.g., 'natural polymeric material', 'container', common preservatives) at a high level of generality typically will not add significantly more to an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a generic 'container' for cells was insufficient to pass Step 2B; conversely, a specifically recited scaffold that improved outcomes could suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claim as a whole when determining whether to apply the nature-product analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For some process or method claims, analyze the claim as a whole to determine whether it is focused on the nature-based product per se or on a practical application/assembly such that the nature-product exception analysis is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: firework assembly claims and methods of treatment were analyzed as focused on assemblies/applications, so marked-difference analysis was not required to conclude ineligibility/eligibility.
